previous_value: When calcium oxide (quicklime, CaO) reacts vigorously with water, it produces calcium hydroxide (slaked lime, Ca(OH)₂) according to: CaO(s) + H₂O(l) → Ca(OH)₂(aq) + Heat (ΔH < 0). This reaction satisfies two classifications: (1) Combination reaction: two individual reactants combine to synthesize a single compound; (2) Exothermic reaction: a large amount of thermal energy is liberated, causing the water to boil and the container to become noticeably hot. Thus, it is an exothermic combination reaction (NCERT Section 1.2.1).
updated_value: Calcium oxide (quicklime) reacts with water to form calcium hydroxide and release heat: CaO(s) + H₂O(l) → Ca(OH)₂(s) + heat. This is a combination reaction because two reactants form one product, and it is exothermic because heat is released. The mixture may become noticeably hot; boiling is not a necessary observation.
rationale: Calcium hydroxide is only sparingly soluble and the claim that water necessarily boils is too strong; use a solid/slurry product and avoid an unsupported observation.

previous_value: Rancidity is the aerial oxidation of unsaturated fats and oils present in food items, producing volatile carboxylic acids and aldehydes that result in an unpleasant rancid odour, foul taste, and loss of nutritional value. To prevent this spoilage, snack manufacturers flush airtight chip bags with unreactive, dry nitrogen (N₂) gas. Nitrogen is chemically inert at ambient temperatures, effectively displacing atmospheric oxygen (O₂) and moisture, thereby halting the oxidative chain reaction and preserving snack crispness and flavor.
updated_value: Rancidity can result from oxidation of fats and oils, producing unpleasant-smelling compounds. Food manufacturers may flush sealed snack packages with nitrogen to displace much of the oxygen and slow oxidative rancidity. Nitrogen flushing does not, by itself, establish that moisture has been removed; moisture control is a separate packaging consideration.
rationale: Nitrogen flushing displaces oxygen; it does not necessarily remove moisture. The prior explanation conflated oxygen displacement with moisture control.

previous_value: When a strip of lead (Pb) metal is placed into an aqueous solution of blue copper(II) chloride (CuCl₂), a single displacement reaction occurs: Pb(s) + CuCl₂(aq) → PbCl₂(aq) + Cu(s). In the standard electrochemical reactivity series, lead is positioned above copper (Pb > Cu), meaning lead has a greater electropositive tendency to lose valence electrons (Pb → Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻). Lead reduces copper ions (Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu), resulting in the formation of colourless soluble lead chloride (PbCl₂) and depositing spongy reddish copper on the lead.
updated_value: Lead is above copper in the reactivity series and can displace copper from copper(II) chloride: Pb(s) + CuCl₂(aq) → PbCl₂(s)↓ + Cu(s). Lead(II) chloride is sparingly soluble in cold water and may form a solid coating; it should not be described as a fully soluble aqueous product. Copper is deposited as a reddish-brown solid.
rationale: Lead(II) chloride is sparingly soluble, not a fully soluble aqueous product; correct the product state and solubility description.

Storing silver bromide in dark amber-coloured or opaque glass bottles filters out actinic wavelengths of light, preventing photochemical decomposition. updated_value: Silver bromide is photosensitive and decomposes on exposure to light: 2AgBr(s) → 2Ag(s) + Br₂. The formation of finely divided metallic silver causes the pale solid to darken. Storing it in a light-protective container reduces exposure and helps prevent this photochemical decomposition.
rationale: The previous explanation overstated immediate bromine release and toxicity in ordinary storage context; retain the balanced photolysis explanation without sensational wording.

previous_value: H⁺ ions are positively charged cations, which migrate to the negatively charged Cathode (-) to form H₂ gas. O²⁻ ions are negatively charged anions, which migrate to the positively charged Anode (+) to form O₂ gas.
updated_value: During electrolysis of acidified water, hydrogen is produced at the cathode (negative electrode) and oxygen at the anode (positive electrode). At the cathode, hydrogen ions are reduced to H₂. At the anode, water is oxidised to O₂; sulphate ions mainly act as spectator ions under these conditions. It is not accurate to describe free oxide ions from water as the species that migrate to and discharge at the anode.
rationale: In aqueous acidified water, oxygen is formed by oxidation of water at the anode; free O²⁻ ions are not the correct explanatory species.

In contrast, NaCl has an extremely strong electrostatic ionic lattice requiring far higher energy (such as electric molten electrolysis) to break.
updated_value: Silver bromide is a photosensitive silver halide. Light can initiate its photochemical decomposition: 2AgBr(s) → 2Ag(s) + Br₂. Sodium chloride does not undergo this photochemical decomposition under ordinary sunlight conditions. The difference should be described in terms of the photosensitivity of silver halides, not as a simple comparison of one bond strength with the ionic lattice energy of sodium chloride.
rationale: The former bond-energy comparison is an oversimplification and does not adequately explain the photochemical selectivity.

previous_value: The gases evolved are sulphur dioxide (SO₂) and sulphur trioxide (SO₃). Both are acidic oxides (they turn moist blue litmus red) and possess the characteristic pungent, suffocating smell of burning sulphur.
updated_value: Strong heating of ferrous sulphate produces sulphur dioxide (SO₂) and sulphur trioxide (SO₃), along with ferric oxide. Both sulphur oxides are acidic oxides and turn moist blue litmus red. These gases are irritating and harmful; they must not be identified by deliberately smelling them. Use an appropriate supervised demonstration and indicator test.
rationale: Add safe testing guidance; do not recommend direct smelling of irritating sulphur oxides.

updated_value: Rancidity can occur when fats and oils are oxidised by oxygen in air. Oxidative breakdown produces unpleasant-smelling compounds, including aldehydes, ketones and some volatile acids, which affect taste and odour. The Reason correctly explains the Assertion. Note that butyric acid in butter is commonly associated with hydrolytic rancidity, so it should not be used as a specific example of oxidative rancidity.
rationale: The previous explanation incorrectly presented butyric acid as an oxidative-rancidity example; distinguish it from hydrolytic rancidity.
